results.title: Exposure-based modeling of operational risk - EverybodyWiki Bios & Wiki
results.content: Exposure-based modeling of operational risk * 2 Background: the triplet definition of risk * 3 Description of the XOI method * 3.1 Definition of components * 3.3 Consistency with the Bowtie representation * 4 Application to operational risk in banking * 4.1 Overview of Operational Risk in Banking * 4.2 Exposure-Based Taxonomy * 4.3 Parallel with credit and market risk * 4.4 Scenario-based quantification of major risks * 4.5.1 Trading error * 4.5.2 Conduct risk / mis-selling **Exposure-based modeling** refers to a class of quantitative risk modeling approaches in which risk is represented as the potential occurrence of adverse events affecting a defined set of exposed units — such as systems, employees, clients, or transactions. It formally separates the definition of exposure units, the conditional probability of adverse events, and their impacts, thereby enabling structured scenario simulation and transparent risk analysis. It applies a formal decomposition of risk into quantifiable components aligned with these theoretical foundations: * a clearly defined object (exposure), * the possibility of an adverse event (occurrence), The approach builds on the CPCU-based concept of vulnerability — understood as the conjunction of peril, object, and consequence — and translates it into a quantitative modeling structure. Bowtie representation of a risk in the XOI approach (Exposure, Occurrence, Impact) The XOI framework also allows for mapping risk control measures onto this structure, with the following correspondences: * **Avoidance**: acts on **Exposure**, aiming to eliminate or reduce the presence of the risk-enabling resource, * **Prevention**: targets the probability of **Occurrence**, addressing root causes or vulnerabilities, * **Protection**: seeks to mitigate **Impact** through containment, backup systems, or insurance. In the context of operational risk modeling, the XOI method can be used to support the construction of a two-dimensional taxonomy based on the intersection of exposed resources and potential adverse events. In the XOI approach, each scenario corresponds to a specific combination of: * a defined **resource** (or asset) exposed to the risk, * a particular type of **adverse event** (or peril), * and a method for estimating the **impact** if the event occurs. _Operational Risk Modelling in Financial Services: The Exposure-Occurrence-Impact Method_.

results.title: Guide to Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis
results.content: # Guide to Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis. It aims to gauge how sensitive Bayesian inferences are to changes in various model parameters and assumptions. Local sensitivity analysis investigates the behavior of the posterior distribution in response to small perturbations in model inputs. Global sensitivity analysis, on the other hand, provides an overview of how variations in model assumptions across a broader domain can influence the posterior distribution. Hence, sensitivity analysis frequently revolves around assessing how different choices of priors or modifications in the likelihood impact the posterior. + Stan: Widely used for Bayesian inference that supports sensitivity analysis through its flexible modeling language. * **Iterative Refinement:** Based on sensitivity results, revisit and refine priors, model structures, or data collection strategies to ensure robust inferences. + **Global Sensitivity:** Employ variance-based measures (i.e., Sobol indices) to assess the overall impact of different prior distributions and likelihood modifications. The sensitivity analysis revealed that the forecast model was particularly influenced by the prior assigned to consumer spending. * **Include Detailed Methodology:** Document every step of the sensitivity analysis process, including the choice of priors, model modifications, and computational strategies. flowchart TD A["Start: Define Bayesian Model"] --> B["Select Key Parameters"] B --> C["Local Sensitivity Analysis"] B --> D["Global Sensitivity Analysis"] C --> E["Compute Influence Functions"] D --> F["Perform Variance-Based Analysis"] E --> G["Aggregate Results"] F --> G G --> H["Visualize Outcomes"] H --> I["Interpret and Report"]. Bayesian sensitivity analysis stands as a critical component in establishing the robustness and credibility of statistical models. By systematically examining how modifications in priors, likelihoods, and other model parameters influence the resulting posterior distributions, analysts can safeguard against overly optimistic or skewed conclusions. Moreover, real-world case studies in medical research and economic forecasting illustrate how sensitivity analysis can inform model adjustments, ultimately leading to more reliable and interpretable results. As the field of Bayesian statistics continues to evolve, so too will the tools and methods available for sensitivity analysis, pushing the boundaries of what robust inference can achieve. By employing robust sensitivity analysis, practitioners can better navigate the complexities inherent in Bayesian modeling and ultimately derive conclusions that are both reliable and well-substantiated.

results.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Priors in the Bayesian Dirichlet Auto-Regressive Moving Average Model
results.content: We examine how prior specification affects the Bayesian Dirichlet Auto-Regressive Moving Average (B-DARMA) model for compositional time series. Bayesian Dirichlet ARMA; compositional time series; forecasting; sensitivity analysis; shrinkage priors; S&P 500 sectors; Stan. In particular, the Bayesian Dirichlet Auto-Regressive Moving Average (B-DARMA) model [9] addresses key compositional modeling challenges by introducing Vector Auto-Regression (VAR) and Vector Moving Average (VMA) terms for multivariate compositional data. In this paper, we systematically investigate how five different prior families—informative normal, horseshoe, Laplace, spike-and-slab, and hierarchical shrinkage—affect parameter recovery and predictive accuracy in the B-DARMA model. In the remainder of this paper, we first review the B-DARMA model (Section 2) and outline how our five prior families (informative, horseshoe, Laplace, spike-and-slab, and hierarchical) encode distinct shrinkage behaviors. The normal prior provides a baseline continuous shrinkage, the horseshoe prior excels when only a minority of parameters are truly large, the Laplace prior induces an -type penalty that can zero out many coefficients, the spike-and-slab prior explicitly discards some parameters, and the hierarchical prior alternative enables group-level learning of shrinkage scales. We conduct three simulation studies to investigate how different priors affect parameter inference and forecasting in a B-DARMA model. The horseshoe, Laplace, and hierarchical priors yield stable forecasts across various parameter settings, whereas the informative normal approach is more susceptible to inflated estimates in large or sparse models. A B-DARMA(10,0) model was fit with each of the five priors using the training data. **Mean RMSE and MAE by model for the S&P 500 analysis.** We aggregate forecast errors across all 11 sectors under each prior. In the large-scale B-DARMA model, shrinkage priors reduced extraneous complexity and lowered forecast errors. Our three simulation studies demonstrated how prior selection interacts with model specification in B-DARMA. When the model order matched the true data-generating process (DARMA(2,1)), all priors yielded acceptable results, although the horseshoe and hierarchical priors produced slightly lower RMSE and better interval coverage. Just as in the overfitting simulation, the horseshoe, Laplace, and spike-and-slab priors effectively shrank extraneous parameters and preserved forecast accuracy. The S&P 500 data analysis underscores these points: the shrinkage priors consistently outperformed the informative prior in managing a high-dimensional model, yet sector-specific volatility still caused reduced accuracy.
